Johannesburg Art Gallery

By: Eugene Botha | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
...............THE BIGGEST ART MUSEUM IN AFRICA LIES IN SHAMBLES

Unique Selling Point:
Part of our National heritage in peril

Summary:
The Johannesburg Art Gallery is an art gallery in Joubert Park in the city centre of Johannesburg, South Africa. It is the largest gallery on the continent. It boasts over 9,000 works of art, displayed in 15 exhibition halls and sculpture gardens. The art is valued at between R500 million and a billion rand. But the Gallery is in total disrepair and in shambles, and this needs to be brought to the public's attention as soon as possible.

Further information:
The Johannesburg Art Gallery is an art gallery in Joubert Park in the city centre of Johannesburg, South Africa.

It is the largest gallery on the continent. It boasts over 9,000 works of art, displayed in 15 exhibition halls and sculpture gardens.

The gallery consists of 15 exhibition halls and sculpture gardens.

It houses collections of 17th-century Dutch paintings (including 39 Rembrandts), 18th- and 19th-century British and European art, 19th-century South African works, a large contemporary collection of 20th-century local and international art, and a print cabinet containing works from the 15th century to the present, including Pablo Picasso, Claude Monet, Gerard Sekoto, Walter Battiss, Rodin, Henry Moore, William Kentridge and Sydney Kumalo and many other local and international artists.

The sandstone building, which was completed in 1915, was designed by Sir Edwin Lutyens is a national heritage building.
BUT TODAY IT IS NOTHING MORE THAN A SHAMBLES, A DUMP.

The building is in total disrepair and crumbling. I was there on Sunday and took the pictures below. Lots and lost of water damage, empty exhibit halls, crumbling walls, closed-off areas.

The building was flooded in 2017 and it seems nothing has been done about this at all, despite a new curator appointed in 2018 --Kwazi Gule.

He said at the time: “ I have seen a number of museums in some of the biggest cities - including Madrid, London, New York and São Paulo, among others - and I think we need to measure up to those international standards.”

But nothing has happened. Four years later it is now even worse and cause for real concern.

It seems that JAG fall under the City of Johannesburg, although the curator seems to be appointed by DAC.
It is extremely difficult to make contact with anybody.

When I visited there on Sunday were two security guards at the entrance. No working CCTV, no other security, outside doors standing open, etc. I could easily have walked out with a number of paintings.

AND THERE WERE NO VISITORS AT ALL!!!

There have been a few media reports on this in recent weeks, but no in-depth investigation, and it seems that the only interviews so far were with Christopher Till, a curator from 1984 to 1992. Nobody has been confronted in any serious manner about the state of JAG and what is being done.

There is a Facebook page called the Friends of Johannesburg Art Gallery, but it seems they can’t do anything and maintains a website and Facebook page. A recent Facebook entry reads:

"Author: Friends of Johannesburg Art Gallery
Tyrone Dunn the best you can do is to contact the City of Johannesburg or tweet about this. There are no telephones nobody answered them anyway. Friends of JAG who manage this page, have no power or any under the current leadership. Our hands are tied. Now it is up to individuals to activate and protest."

All of this requires some serious investigation, with the following questions being asked:
• Who is actually responsible for JAG -- the building and the collection?
• Who is the curator? Is it still Kwazi Gule? His name is mentioned nowhere anymore.
• Why is there no maintenance? Is it the responsibility of the City of Jo’burg?
• Where are the other art works being stored – the basement was flooded in 2017 and that is where the storerooms are.
• Are the 9000 priceless art works safe – are they still there? There must be catalogue and one can surely easily check to see if thye have not benn pilfered?
• Are there any immediate future plans with JAG?
• Why is there virtually no security measures?
• Is the location in the middle of downtown Johannesburg still viable?
• The “Friends of Jag” collected funds for the Gallery in the past. What has happened to these funds? (“With the help from the Friends of JAG, the Johannesburg Art Gallery can maintain its collection of Picassos and Rodins, Sekotos and Pierneefs. Together, the #FRIENDSOFJAG find innovative ways to raise funds for the gallery’s activities and educational programmes.)

TREATMENT
There are a number of aspects that needs attention:
* The crumbling building -- inside and out. Will need drone footage as well.
* The flood damage -- lower levels. Can only gain access through management.
* The poor security -- we will take in a painting, ut it up and also remove it to show that it is possible to smuggle out artworks.
* We would need a catalogue of all artwork in the gallery, and check if it is still there.
* The current curator must be confronted about the state of the gallery.
* The City of Johannesburg must be confronted about the state of the Gallery.
* Art experts must be consulted about the conditions in which priceless artworks are supposed to be kept.

Script:


V/O:
The Johannesburg Art Gallery – lying at the southern end of Joubert Park – in the heart of downtown Johannesburg.

It’s home to the most significant collection of art on the continent.
Karel:
The Pre-Raphaelites, Rembrandt, Picasso, Francis Bacon, Picasso, Marcel Douchant. ….young emerging artists right from 1920’s and 40’s and that material is here and on top of that is the greatest collection of early Zulu, Shangaan, and Tsonga material in the world.

V/O:
Increasingly, though, there’ve been reports that this precious collection may not be in safe hands. With such an important artistic heritage at stake, we decided to investigate.

The celebrated sculpture garden greets our arrival. But it’s overgrown and littered with rubbish. The building’s exterior is clearly in dire need of repair and maintenance.
Brian:
I think it is constant neglect.
V/O:
Brian McKechnie is a heritage architect working on restoring historical buildings in Johannesburg.
Brian:
The gallery itself is disintegrating, and ja, it is not an ideal space to view artworks
V/O:
Inside, the neglect continues: not what you’d expect from a gallery housing around 10 000 artworks, including Rembrants and Monets.

The majority of exhibition spaces are empty, paint peeling from the walls.
Bongani:
It is a Friday afternoon, it is the middle of the day. This should be teeming with visitors, with buses from schools, people coming from all over the country to see this famous collection… can you hear the echo?
V/O:
We’re joined by Karel Nel – an internationally renowned artist and author – who’s been associated with the Gallery for many years. He’s angry that it no longer attracts visitors - so different from major art galleries elsewhere in the world.
Karel Nel:
People stand in queues to get in. Here the largest number of visitors are most probably the JMPD coming to use the toilets, you know….which is a tragedy.
V/O:
Apart from the lack of art on display, the occasional visitor is confronted by utter disarray – almost every corner is littered with rubbish and building material, bird droppings on windows and stairs. There’s an air of neglect that - it would appear - also extends to the security.
Karel:
The building is threadbare the staff is threadbare, there is no security in the galleries
V/O:
To test the impact of that, we arrange a heist… with a twist. We smuggle a cheap landscape we bought from a pawnshop for twenty-five rand into the building. Inside, we assemble a hastily-cut frame, and hang it in the gallery. A few days later, we return and “steal” it.
Link:
So how were we able to walk in, put an artwork, leave it there, come back and collect it without any one noticing? Well, some of the worker have told us that the security cameras are out of order.
V/O:
While our intentions were honourable, we weren’t the only ones able to make off with an artwork. Since the year 2000 about 15 pieces have been stolen, with only two ever recovered.

Christopher Till is an art expert and former Director at the Johannesburg Art Gallery.
Till:
I was staggered to see the chaos. The gallery spaces had been cannibalized to just be junk stores.
V/O:
Hidden away in an upstairs room, we stumble upon a large number of works from the contemporary art collection.
Bongani:
Having seen mostly empty walls, this seems is where the bulk of the collection is kept. They are really piled on top of each other, it is not in a controlled environment, it probably gets warm in here, there is no climate control and this is the largest, the most significant, the most valuable collection of art on the continent. I mean some of it, look… just lying here. Just lying here.
V/O:
The reason these paintings aren’t on display is down to another of the gallery’s problems: water leakage. It appears to be slowly destroying the entire building.
Bongani:
This seems to be the old conservation room, but as you can see there has been massive damage, particular to the floors. It used to be parquet flooring but it has been so severely damaged that it feels as if there has been a fire. There hasn’t, but that is the extent of the damage.
Brian:
If you look at the condition …. long period of neglect.
V/O:
The building and a foundation collection of artworks were donated to the people of Johannesburg in 1915 and the City of Johannesburg was appointed as custodian.

In 1986 Anglo American funded an extension to the original building and added this whole section with copper domes.
Flo:
Unfortunately from day one that building has leaked.
V/O:
Flo Bird, a heritage activist who heads the Johannesburg Heritage Foundation, says the new addition was problematic from the start.
Flo:
The City secretary didn’t even want to pay them for the work because it was always leaking.
TILL:
And the architect blamed the builder and the builder blamed the architect and then the builder went bankrupt and nothing really was done to deal with this water problem.
V/O:
The leaking roof hasn’t only compromised the building’s structure, several irreplaceable artworks have also been severely damaged – they include works by Dutch Masters as well as Irma Stern, Gregoire Boonzaaier, Walter Battis and others.

After more than a century under its care, it’s clear the City of Johannesburg has failed dismally as custodian of the gallery.
Christopher Till:
It is an abomination

Flo Bird:
It looks like a war zone. I mean it is ghastly when you go into some parts of it.

Karel:
It is morally reprehensible.

Brian
It is a health and safety hazard. You probably should not have members of the public in a building like that.
V/O:
There was significant flooding in the building in 2016 and the persistent damp since then has seen black mold forming in various parts of the gallery, forcing their closure for health reasons.

And for the last 7 years no new artworks have been added to the collection.
Karel:
We put an embargo on buying any more work, because it just gets damaged.
V/O:
In a written response the City of Johannesburg acknowledges the problems with the leaking roof, saying it’s taking steps to address the issues.
Bongani:
You would think that something like a leaking roof could be sorted out though?

Brian:
It sounds like a really simple problem to rectify. The city apparently has spent money on trying to rectify these issues, and it also most seems like where the touched the gallery they made it worse.
V/O:
The City didn’t comment on the security issues, stating only that it has done an assessment and will be addressing the problems identified.

It says artworks are stored in the upstairs room because there isn’t enough suitable leak-free storage space, AND that 24 paintings have been damaged by water.
Flo:
There were quotes on restoring and repairing, and that work was never done.
V/O:
This is a quotation for around two hundred thousand rand submitted to repair the works in 2018. Despite the significant value of the paintings involved, the City of Johannesburg chose not to accept the quote.

From what we’ve seen, those calling for immediate and urgent action have a strong argument. But what can be done?
Till:
For me that give grounds for that collection to be taken away from the City of Johannesburg because they are not looking after it.
Karel:
We need to primarily move the collection into safety so that it is carefully looked after and that it is in the proper climatic conditions.
V/O:
Responding to our questions about the poor state of the Gallery building, the City says it spent a million rand on an assessment and condition report last year. New heritage architects have been appointed and funding and renovation options are currently being explored..

However, our requests for that condition report, detailed renovation strategy and the associated costs were declined.

Bongani:
Can it be fixed?

Brian:
Absolutely. You can fix anything. Obviously if you have the right budget.

Bongani:
What would it take to do so?

Brian:
I would imagine you are looking…. I think the one figure I saw was in the region of two hundred and fifty million rand. You are probably looking a little North of that.
V/O:
While confidential plans are hatched behind closed doors, with every passing day the building continues its sorry decline, and one of the most unique art collections in the world remains at the mercy of the elements.
***




PROMO 1 11”

The largest art collection in Africa lies forgotten in a crumbling building, with persistent water leaks damaging priceless artworks. What has become of the Johannesburg Art Gallery?


PROMO 2 21”

Rembrandt, Monet and Picasso - names associated with the world’s finest museums and galleries. But here in Johannesburg their masterpieces are hidden and neglected in a rotting, derelict building.

Brian
It is a health and safety hazard. You probably should not have members of the public in a building like that.

Will we lose this treasure forever?


PROMO 3 21”

The Johannesburg Art Gallery boasts an impressive collection of over 10,000 artworks - from early Dutch masters to contemporary African works… But there’s a problem…

Flo Bird:
It looks like a war zone. I mean it is ghastly when you go into some parts of it.

What will it take to restore the gallery to its former glory?

V/O: The City didn’t comment on the security issues, stating only that it has done an assessment and will be addressing the problems identified. It says artworks are stored in the upstairs room because there isn’t enough suitable leak-free storage space, AND that 24 paintings have been damaged by water. Flo: There were quotes on restoring and repairing, and that work was never done. V/O: This is a quotation for around two hundred thousand rand submitted to repair the works in 2018. Despite the significant value of the paintings involved, the City of Johannesburg chose not to accept the quote. From what we’ve seen, those calling for immediate and urgent action have a strong argument. But what can be done? Till: For me that give grounds for that collection to be taken away from the City of Johannesburg because they are not looking after it. Karel: We need to primarily move the collection into safety so that it is carefully looked after and that it is in the proper climatic conditions. V/O: Responding to our questions about the poor state of the Gallery building, the City says it spent a million rand on an assessment and condition report last year. New heritage architects have been appointed and funding and renovation options are currently being explored.. However, our requests for that condition report, detailed renovation strategy and the associated costs were declined. Bongani: Can it be fixed? Brian: Absolutely. You can fix anything. Obviously if you have the right budget. Bongani: What would it take to do so? Brian: I would imagine you are looking…. I think the one figure I saw was in the region of two hundred and fifty million rand. You are probably looking a little North of that. V/O: While confidential plans are hatched behind closed doors, with every passing day the building continues its sorry decline, and one of the most unique art collections in the world remains at the mercy of the elements. *** PROMO 1 11” The largest art collection in Africa lies forgotten in a crumbling building, with persistent water leaks damaging priceless artworks. What has become of the Johannesburg Art Gallery? PROMO 2 21” Rembrandt, Monet and Picasso - names associated with the world’s finest museums and galleries. But here in Johannesburg their masterpieces are hidden and neglected in a rotting, derelict building. Brian It is a health and safety hazard. You probably should not have members of the public in a building like that. Will we lose this treasure forever? PROMO 3 21” The Johannesburg Art Gallery boasts an impressive collection of over 10,000 artworks - from early Dutch masters to contemporary African works… But there’s a problem… Flo Bird: It looks like a war zone. I mean it is ghastly when you go into some parts of it. What will it take to restore the gallery to its former glory?

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): ...............THE BIGGEST ART MUSEUM IN AFRICA LIES IN SHAMBLES
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Part of our National heritage in peril
metadata.Summary: The Johannesburg Art Gallery is an art gallery in Joubert Park in the city centre of Johannesburg, South Africa. It is the largest gallery on the continent. It boasts over 9,000 works of art, displayed in 15 exhibition halls and sculpture gardens. The art is valued at between R500 million and a billion rand. But the Gallery is in total disrepair and in shambles, and this needs to be brought to the public's attention as soon as possible.
metadata.Further information: The Johannesburg Art Gallery is an art gallery in Joubert Park in the city centre of Johannesburg, South Africa. It is the largest gallery on the continent. It boasts over 9,000 works of art, displayed in 15 exhibition halls and sculpture gardens. The gallery consists of 15 exhibition halls and sculpture gardens. It houses collections of 17th-century Dutch paintings (including 39 Rembrandts), 18th- and 19th-century British and European art, 19th-century South African works, a large contemporary collection of 20th-century local and international art, and a print cabinet containing works from the 15th century to the present, including Pablo Picasso, Claude Monet, Gerard Sekoto, Walter Battiss, Rodin, Henry Moore, William Kentridge and Sydney Kumalo and many other local and international artists. The sandstone building, which was completed in 1915, was designed by Sir Edwin Lutyens is a national heritage building. BUT TODAY IT IS NOTHING MORE THAN A SHAMBLES, A DUMP. The building is in total disrepair and crumbling. I was there on Sunday and took the pictures below. Lots and lost of water damage, empty exhibit halls, crumbling walls, closed-off areas. The building was flooded in 2017 and it seems nothing has been done about this at all, despite a new curator appointed in 2018 --Kwazi Gule. He said at the time: “ I have seen a number of museums in some of the biggest cities - including Madrid, London, New York and São Paulo, among others - and I think we need to measure up to those international standards.” But nothing has happened. Four years later it is now even worse and cause for real concern. It seems that JAG fall under the City of Johannesburg, although the curator seems to be appointed by DAC. It is extremely difficult to make contact with anybody. When I visited there on Sunday were two security guards at the entrance. No working CCTV, no other security, outside doors standing open, etc. I could easily have walked out with a number of paintings. AND THERE WERE NO VISITORS AT ALL!!! There have been a few media reports on this in recent weeks, but no in-depth investigation, and it seems that the only interviews so far were with Christopher Till, a curator from 1984 to 1992. Nobody has been confronted in any serious manner about the state of JAG and what is being done. There is a Facebook page called the Friends of Johannesburg Art Gallery, but it seems they can’t do anything and maintains a website and Facebook page. A recent Facebook entry reads: "Author: Friends of Johannesburg Art Gallery Tyrone Dunn the best you can do is to contact the City of Johannesburg or tweet about this. There are no telephones nobody answered them anyway. Friends of JAG who manage this page, have no power or any under the current leadership. Our hands are tied. Now it is up to individuals to activate and protest." All of this requires some serious investigation, with the following questions being asked: • Who is actually responsible for JAG -- the building and the collection? • Who is the curator? Is it still Kwazi Gule? His name is mentioned nowhere anymore. • Why is there no maintenance? Is it the responsibility of the City of Jo’burg? • Where are the other art works being stored – the basement was flooded in 2017 and that is where the storerooms are. • Are the 9000 priceless art works safe – are they still there? There must be catalogue and one can surely easily check to see if thye have not benn pilfered? • Are there any immediate future plans with JAG? • Why is there virtually no security measures? • Is the location in the middle of downtown Johannesburg still viable? • The “Friends of Jag” collected funds for the Gallery in the past. What has happened to these funds? (“With the help from the Friends of JAG, the Johannesburg Art Gallery can maintain its collection of Picassos and Rodins, Sekotos and Pierneefs. Together, the #FRIENDSOFJAG find innovative ways to raise funds for the gallery’s activities and educational programmes.) TREATMENT There are a number of aspects that needs attention: * The crumbling building -- inside and out. Will need drone footage as well. * The flood damage -- lower levels. Can only gain access through management. * The poor security -- we will take in a painting, ut it up and also remove it to show that it is possible to smuggle out artworks. * We would need a catalogue of all artwork in the gallery, and check if it is still there. * The current curator must be confronted about the state of the gallery. * The City of Johannesburg must be confronted about the state of the Gallery. * Art experts must be consulted about the conditions in which priceless artworks are supposed to be kept.
